title: Deterministic photon waveform adaptation for quantum connectivity
authors: Jeffrey Mohan, Jérémy Berroir, Filippo Borselli, David Libault, Ferhat Loubar, Kilian Müller, Jed Rowland, Félix Hoffet, Eleni Diamanti, Tom Darras, Tommaso Mazzoni, Julien Laurat
abstract: The scalability of quantum technologies will depend on the ability to interconnect independent quantum systems through photonic channels. However, heterogeneous quantum platforms emit and absorb photons with widely differing properties, severely limiting inter-node interference and modular connectivity. Here we demonstrate a cold-atom optical quantum memory that simultaneously achieves near-unity storage-and-retrieval efficiency and deterministic temporal adaptation of single photons between arbitrary and programmable input and output pulse waveforms. Operating at high optical depth and within a fully integrated architecture, the system can store photons with durations spanning over three orders of magnitude and reshape them arbitrarily without compromising efficiency, achieving compatibility with many current platforms. By augmenting the role of a quantum memory from a passive storage element to an active programmable photonic interface, our results establish a key building block for scalable entanglement-based quantum networks and modular quantum computing architectures.
summary: This paper demonstrates a cold-atom quantum memory that acts as a programmable photonic interface, solving the challenge of connecting quantum systems with mismatched photon properties. By using optimal control theory, the system can deterministically reshape stored single-photon pulses to match any desired output waveform. This capability establishes a key building block for scalable, modular quantum networks and computing architectures.
main_problem: Scalability of quantum technologies requires interconnecting independent quantum systems, which is limited by the differing photonic properties of heterogeneous quantum platforms.
main_result: The system achieves deterministic and programmable temporal adaptation of single-photon pulses while maintaining near-unity storage-and-retrieval efficiency.
method: Optimal control theory is used to dynamically modulate the pulse group velocity in a cold-atom memory, allowing reshaping of the retrieved photon waveform.
model_or_system: The platform is a cold-atom optical quantum memory using Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) in a $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ ensemble, functioning as an active, programmable photonic interface.
key_observables: Storage-and-retrieval efficiency ($\eta$), conditional overlap ($I_c$), and the ability to reshape output waveforms to match arbitrary target profiles.
important_parameters: Storage durations spanning over three orders of magnitude; the control field power $P_c(t)$ is the key tunable parameter.
main_assumptions: The system requires ultra-high optical depth and low temperature for high efficiency, and the control mechanism relies on engineering the control beam power $P_c(t)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the concept of reshaping incompatible waveforms for quantum interconnects, the integrated system setup, and demonstrations of bandwidth adaptation and arbitrary waveform generation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for quantum interconnects, presents the cold-atom memory as an active interface, details the use of optimal control to achieve deterministic waveform reshaping, and demonstrates high efficiency across wide bandwidths.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical hardware bottleneck in quantum networking by transforming a passive storage element into an active, programmable quantum interface, which is highly relevant for quantum information processing.
